1.topic: Playing a character and writing a short script
1.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. prepare to play a character using motivation, voice, body and projection;
2. perform an improvised or scripted scene with a partner;
3. write a short original script in the correct format;
4. evaluate a performance using agreed criteria.

## Materials

A printed scene from a recommended text or a teacher-made scene (a danfo conductor and a passenger), blank paper, a marker board.

## Starter

Show two learners a one-line scene: 'You said you would pay me back.' Ask each to perform it three ways (angry, sad, joking). Discuss how voice and body changed the meaning.

## Development

1. Motivation: what the character wants in the scene. Ask 'What do I want? What stops me?'.
2. Voice: pitch, speed, loudness, pause. Body: posture, gesture, facial expression, movement. Projection: speaking so the whole audience hears, without shouting.
3. Listening and reacting: acting is reacting. A line should answer what the other character just did.
4. Script format: scene heading (place and time); character name, then a colon, then the line; stage directions in brackets.
5. A scene needs a beginning, a problem and an ending.
6. Perform for the class and evaluate: Was the character clear? Was the voice clear? Was the scene believable?

## Class activity

Pairs prepare and perform the danfo scene, swap roles, then write a six-line original scene in correct script format.

## Evaluation

1. What is motivation in acting?
2. Why should actors project?
3. How is a character's name written in a script?

## Assignment

Problem set on the app. Write a six-line scene of your own and mark the stage directions in brackets.

reading.title: Acting, and writing it down
reading.content:
# Playing a character and writing a short script

## Playing a character

A good actor does not just say lines. The actor becomes someone else for the scene.

**Motivation.** Ask: *What does my character want in this scene? What stops them?* A conductor in a danfo wants his fare. A passenger who has already paid wants to be believed. These wants drive everything.

**Voice.** Change pitch (high or low), speed (fast or slow), loudness and pauses to show feeling. A scared character may speak fast and high; a confident one slowly and low. A **pause** before an important line builds attention.

**Body.** Posture, gesture and expression show who the character is. A tired old man walks slowly with a bent back. An angry conductor leans forward with his hand out.

**Projection.** The back row of the audience must hear you. Projecting does not mean shouting; it means using your breath and clear speech so the sound carries. Speaking with your back to the audience hides your voice and face.

**Listening and reacting.** Acting is reacting. Listen to the other actor, and let your line answer what they just did.

## Writing a short script

A script has a standard format.

SCENE: A classroom in Ibadan, early morning.

TEACHER: (looking at the clock) Tunde, assembly finished thirty minutes ago.

TUNDE: (breathing hard) Good morning, ma. My mother fell sick and I had to take her to the clinic first.

- The **scene heading** gives the place and time.
- The **character's name** comes before each line, followed by a colon.
- **Stage directions** go in brackets and say how a line is spoken or what the character does.
- **Dialogue** is what the characters say. It should fit the character.

## Shape of a scene

A scene needs:

1. A **beginning:** who, where and what is happening.
2. A **problem:** something is wanted or goes wrong.
3. An **ending:** the problem is solved, or a new problem appears.

## Evaluating a performance

Ask: Could I tell who the character was? Could I hear every word? Did the actors listen to each other? Did the scene have a clear beginning, problem and ending?

2.topic: Making a film and a school production: stages, jobs and budgets
2.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe pre-production, production and post-production in film;
2. match jobs to stages;
3. prepare and total a simple production budget;
4. describe how to train for a career in drama or film.

## Materials

A call sheet or a production schedule (teacher-made), calculators, a marker board.

## Starter

Ask: if your class wanted to make a ten-minute film, what would you do first, second and last? List their ideas on the board.

## Development

1. Pre-production: planning. The script is written, the budget made, actors cast, locations chosen and a schedule set. Key jobs: producer, scriptwriter, director, casting director.
2. Production: filming. The director, cinematographer, sound recordist, actors, makeup and costume crews work on set.
3. Post-production: after filming. The editor joins the shots, music and sound are added, colours corrected, and the film is distributed (cinema, television, online).
4. A budget lists expected costs. Work a school budget: costumes ₦35,000, set ₦48,000, printing ₦12,000, lighting ₦25,000, refreshments ₦20,000. Total and compare with money raised.
5. Training: school drama club, community theatre, film schools and university Theatre Arts programmes, internships on productions.

## Class activity

Groups make a plan and a budget for a short film, listing jobs for each stage and totalling their costs.

## Evaluation

1. In which stage does the editor work?
2. What is a budget?
3. Name two ways a young person can train for film.

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app. Choose a short story and list the jobs and costs to film it.

reading.title: From idea to screen: the work behind a film
reading.content:
# Making a film and a production budget

Every film, from a small school film to a big Nollywood production, goes through three stages.

## 1. Pre-production

Pre-production is **planning**. Nothing is filmed yet.

- The **scriptwriter** writes the script.
- The **producer** raises the money and makes the **budget**.
- The **casting director** chooses actors.
- The **director** plans how the film will look.
- **Locations** are found and a **schedule** is made.

## 2. Production

Production is **filming**. The crew goes to the locations.

- The **director** guides the actors and the crew.
- The **cinematographer** operates the camera.
- The **sound recordist** records speech and sound.
- **Actors**, **makeup artists** and **costume** staff work to the schedule.

## 3. Post-production

Post-production is **after filming**.

- The **editor** cuts and joins the shots to tell the story.
- **Music** and **sound effects** are added.
- **Colour** is corrected.
- The film is **distributed**: shown in cinemas, on television or online.

## The budget

A **budget** is a list of expected costs. Without one, a production may run out of money.

**Worked example.** A school drama club plans a play. Costs: costumes ₦35,000; set materials ₦48,000; posters and programmes ₦12,000; lighting hire ₦25,000; refreshments ₦20,000.

Total = 35,000 + 48,000 + 12,000 + 25,000 + 20,000 = ₦140,000.

The club has raised ₦120,000, so it is short by 140,000 - 120,000 = ₦20,000.

To close the gap, the club can **cut costs** (borrow costumes, make the set from waste cardboard) and **raise money** (sell tickets, find a sponsor).

## Training for a career

- Join the school drama club and the community theatre.
- Study Theatre Arts or film at a university or film school.
- Work as an assistant on productions to learn on the job.
- Make short films with a phone and show them to others.

A career in drama is built by practice, patience and teamwork.

3.topic: The rehearsal process: from reading to dress rehearsal
3.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. name the stages of rehearsal in order and say what happens in each;
2. explain rehearsal rules and why they matter;
3. take part in a structured rehearsal of a school play;
4. state the stage manager's job in rehearsal.

## Materials

A short play script for the class, a rehearsal schedule on a chart, chairs for a rehearsal stage, a marker board.

## Starter

Ask: why do footballers train before a match? Why should actors rehearse before an audience comes? Take answers.

## Development

1. Stage 1, read-through: the cast read the whole script aloud together. Stage 2, blocking: the director plans where actors stand and move.
2. Stage 3, working rehearsals: scenes are practised again and again, characters are developed, and actors learn their lines (off-book, meaning without the script in hand).
3. Stage 4, run-throughs: whole acts or the whole play without stopping.
4. Stage 5, technical rehearsal: lights, sound and set changes are practised with the crew. Stage 6, dress rehearsal: everything is done as in the show, with full costume and makeup.
5. The stage manager keeps the prompt book (the master script with all cues and blocking) and the schedule.
6. Rehearsal rules: be on time; learn lines by the date set; listen to notes; switch off phones; warm up; respect others.

## Class activity

The class rehearses the first scene of a short play, from read-through to a mini run-through, following the stages and rules.

## Evaluation

1. What is a read-through?
2. What does 'off-book' mean?
3. Which rehearsal includes full costume and makeup?

## Assignment

Worksheet on the app. Write a six-week rehearsal plan for a short school play.

reading.title: How a play gets ready
reading.content:
# The rehearsal process

No good play appears by chance. Weeks of rehearsal come before the opening night. Rehearsals follow stages.

## The stages of rehearsal

1. **Read-through.** The cast sit and read the whole script aloud together. They learn the story, the characters and how the scenes join.
2. **Blocking.** The director plans where actors stand and move in each scene, and the actors write their movements in their scripts.
3. **Working rehearsals.** Scenes are practised again and again. Actors develop their characters and learn their lines. When actors can say their lines without holding the script, they are **off-book**.
4. **Run-throughs.** Whole acts, then the whole play, are performed without stopping, so that the cast learn the pace and the order.
5. **Technical rehearsal.** The crew and cast practise the lights, sound and set changes. It may be slow, because each **cue** (the signal to start a light, sound or action) is practised.
6. **Dress rehearsal.** Everything is done as in the real show, with full costume, makeup, lights and sound. The director gives final notes.

After the dress rehearsal come the opening night and the performances.

## The stage manager

The **stage manager** keeps the **prompt book**, the master copy of the script with all the cues and blocking written in. The stage manager makes the schedule, calls the cast for rehearsals and runs the show from backstage.

## Rehearsal rules

- **Arrive on time.** When one person is late, everyone waits, and time is lost.
- **Learn your lines** by the date the director sets, so that rehearsals can move on from reading to acting.
- **Listen to notes** and try them without arguing. The notes make the play better.
- **Switch off phones**, which disturb the scene and the actors' concentration.
- **Warm up** your body and voice so that nobody is hurt.
- **Respect the other actors.** Be quiet when they rehearse, because they need to concentrate and feel safe to try new things.

## Planning for a school play

A play planned for six weeks might use: read-through and blocking in week 1; scene work and learning lines in weeks 2 and 3; run-throughs in weeks 4 and 5; technical and dress rehearsals in the last days of week 6.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. define dance and name its four elements: body, space, time and energy;
2. describe traditional, modern and creative dance;
3. give examples of Nigerian traditional dances and of modern styles;
4. use the elements of dance to show a feeling.

## Materials

Clips or pictures of Bata, Atilogwu, Swange and Ekombi dancers; a drum or recorded music; an open space.

Play three short drum rhythms (fast, slow, stop-and-start). Ask learners to move freely to each. Ask: what changed in your body and why?

1. Dance is the art of moving the body in rhythm, usually to music, to express an idea, feeling or story.
2. Elements: body (what moves and how), space (where: direction, size, levels), time (tempo, rhythm) and energy (strong, light, sharp, smooth).
3. Traditional dance is handed down in a community, with set steps, costume and music, and a meaning: for festivals, worship, weddings and rites. Examples: Bata (Yoruba), Atilogwu (Igbo), Swange (Tiv), Ekombi (Efik).

5. Creative dance: dancers invent their own movements to express an idea, with no fixed steps.

Learners are given a feeling (joy, fear, calm) and, in groups, use body, space, time and energy to show it in a 30-second creative dance.

2. What makes a dance traditional?

reading.content:
# Types of dance

**Dance** is the art of moving the body in rhythm, usually to music, to express an idea, a feeling or a story.

## The elements of dance

Every dance, however it looks, is made from four elements.

- **Body:** what moves (arms, feet, head, whole body) and how.
- **Space:** where the dancer moves: forwards, backwards, in a circle, high, middle or low.
- **Time:** the speed and rhythm: fast or slow, steady or broken.
- **Energy:** the force of the movement: strong or light, sharp or smooth.

A dancer showing joy might jump high (space), move fast (time), use bouncy, strong movements (energy) and open the arms wide (body).

## Traditional dance

Traditional dances belong to a community. They are handed down from older people to younger ones. They have set steps, costume and music, and they carry a **meaning**. They are performed at festivals, weddings, funerals, harvests and religious ceremonies.

- **Bata:** a Yoruba dance with fast footwork to the bata drums, linked in tradition to the worship of Sango.
- **Atilogwu:** a lively Igbo dance with quick, athletic movements.
- **Swange:** a Tiv dance from Benue State, danced at social gatherings.
- **Ekombi:** an Efik dance from Cross River with graceful movements and raffia skirts.

## Modern or contemporary dance

Modern dance includes styles such as **ballet**, **jazz**, **hip-hop** and **contemporary dance**. Many began outside Nigeria. They are taught in studios and schools and performed on stage and in music videos. Many Nigerian dancers combine them with traditional movements to make new styles.

## Creative dance

In **creative dance** the dancers invent their own movements to express an idea, such as a storm, a market or a sunrise. There are no fixed steps, so every group's dance is different. Creative dance builds imagination and teamwork.

## Learning to dance with respect

Learn the meaning of a traditional dance before you perform it. A dance may be sacred to a community, and it should be performed with the right costume, music and attitude.

reading.content:
# The choreographer and choreography

## Who is a choreographer?

A **choreographer** creates and arranges dances. The art of arranging dance is called **choreography**. A choreographer decides what movements will be done, in what order, by whom and to what music.

## Steps in making a dance

1. **Choose an idea and music.** The idea may be a harvest, a market or a storm. The music should suit it.
2. **Create movement phrases.** A phrase is a short sequence of steps. Phrases are usually counted in **eights**: "1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8".
3. **Plan the shape of the dance.** Decide the **formations**, the **levels** and the **patterns**.
4. **Teach and rehearse.** The choreographer teaches the dancers part by part.
5. **Refine.** Polish the weak parts, check the timing and add costume and lighting.

## Terms to know

- **Unison:** all the dancers do the same movement at the same time. It looks strong and shows unity.
- **Canon:** the same movement is done by different dancers one after another, like a ripple across the stage. It adds interest and depth.
- **Formation:** how the dancers are arranged: a circle, a line, two rows or a block.
- **Levels:** how high or low the dancers are: high (standing tall or jumping), medium, or low (crouching or on the floor).
- **Pattern:** the path made on the floor, such as a zigzag or a spiral.

## Counting a dance

Music has a steady **tempo**, measured in beats per minute. If the music is 120 beats a minute and the dance lasts 2 minutes:

- Total beats = 120 x 2 = 240.
- Sets of eight = 240 ÷ 8 = 30.

A short dance of four sets of eight has 32 counts.

## An example

A harvest dance: Set 1, all dancers in a line do a stepping pattern in unison (counts 1 to 8). Set 2, dancers form a circle and clap (9 to 16). Set 3, a canon in which each dancer starts a reaching movement one count after the last (17 to 24). Set 4, all return to unison and finish with a pose (25 to 32).

## A good choreographer

A choreographer has ideas, listens to the dancers, teaches clearly and stays patient during rehearsal.

reading.title: Dancing for a living
reading.content:
# Careers in dance

Dance is both an art and a profession.

## Careers in dance

| Career | What the person does |
| --- | --- |
| Professional dancer | Performs on stage, in films, in music videos or with a company |
| Choreographer | Creates and arranges dances |
| Dance teacher | Trains learners in schools and studios |
| Troupe director | Leads a dance company and plans its performances |
| Dance critic or writer | Watches dance and writes about it |
| Costume designer | Makes costumes that suit the dance and let dancers move freely |
| Dance fitness instructor | Leads dance-based exercise classes |
| Dance therapist | Uses movement to help people heal, in clinics and schools |

## Where dancers work

- **Cultural troupes.** The National Troupe of Nigeria is a government company that performs Nigerian dance and drama at home and abroad. State arts councils also keep troupes that perform at festivals and state events.
- **Dance companies and schools,** private and public.
- **Television, film and music videos.**
- **Hotels and cultural centres,** where visitors come to watch Nigerian dances.
- **Churches and schools,** which employ dancers and dance teachers.

## Skills a dancer needs

Rhythm, memory (for long sequences), fitness, flexibility, discipline, teamwork and creativity.

## How to train

1. Join a school or community dance group.
2. Take lessons from a trained teacher.
3. Study Dance or Theatre Arts for a diploma or degree.
4. Attend workshops and work as an apprentice with a company.

## Looking after your body

A dancer's body is the instrument. To keep it healthy:

- **Warm up** before dancing and **cool down** afterwards, so that the muscles are not injured.
- **Drink water** before, during and after dancing.
- **Eat well** and **rest**.
- **Do not dance through pain.** An injury that is ignored can end a career.

Many dancers also have a second skill, such as teaching or costume making, so that they can earn between performances.

## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. describe a traditional Nigerian dance: its people, occasion, music, costume and movements;
2. explain why the meaning of a traditional dance must be learned before it is performed;
3. prepare and perform a short traditional dance with a group;
4. evaluate a performance for rhythm, accuracy and respect.

## Materials

Drums or recorded music for a traditional dance, costume pieces (wrappers, raffia, beads), a space for dancing, clips of Bata, Atilogwu, Ekombi and Swange.

## Starter

Play a traditional rhythm and ask learners to listen without moving. Ask: what kind of dance does this music ask for, and why?

## Development

1. Choose a dance of your own or a neighbouring culture. Find out the people, occasion and meaning from an elder, a cultural teacher or a reliable source.
2. Learn the basic steps slowly with counts and with the drum rhythm, then put them together in a short sequence.
3. Costume: wear what suits the dance and the meaning, and what allows free movement.
4. Formation and expression: dancers keep their lines or circles, and show the energy and feeling of the dance with the face and body.
5. Perform with pride and respect, and then evaluate: Did we keep the rhythm? Were the steps accurate? Did we show respect for the dance?

## Class activity

Groups learn a short sequence of a traditional dance from a guest dancer or video and perform it to the class with live drums or recorded music.

## Evaluation

1. Why should you find out the meaning of a dance before performing it?
2. Name two parts of a traditional dance besides the steps.
3. What should drummers and dancers do together?

reading.title: Dancing the heritage
reading.content:
# Performing traditional Nigerian dance

Traditional dances carry history and meaning. To perform one is to take part in the life of a community, so it must be done with understanding and respect.

## Features of a traditional dance

Every traditional dance has:

- **People:** the community or group it belongs to.
- **Occasion:** when it is performed, such as a festival, wedding, funeral, harvest or religious rite.
- **Music:** the drums, gongs, shakers, flutes and songs that accompany it.
- **Costume:** the clothes, beads, raffia and other items worn.
- **Movement:** the steps, gestures and style.
- **Meaning:** what the dance says or celebrates.

## Some examples

- **Bata** is a dance of the Yoruba, performed to the double-headed bata drums. It has fast, sharp footwork, and in tradition it is linked to the worship of Sango.
- **Atilogwu** is an Igbo dance with quick, acrobatic movements, danced by young people at festivals and celebrations.
- **Ekombi** is an Efik dance from Cross River State, with graceful, swaying movements and beautiful costumes of raffia skirts and beads.
- **Swange** is a Tiv dance from Benue State, danced at social gatherings and ceremonies.

## Preparing to perform

1. **Find out** the people, the occasion and the meaning of the dance.
2. **Learn the steps** from someone who knows the dance well, such as an elder or a cultural teacher, slowly at first and then to the music.
3. **Practise with the drums** so that dancers and drummers keep the same beat and respond to each other.
4. **Choose the right costume**, one that suits the dance and lets you move freely.
5. **Rehearse the formation** and the expression, so the group looks and feels together.
6. **Perform with pride and respect.**

## Why respect matters

Some dances are sacred to a community. Changing them without understanding can cause offence. A creative new dance can borrow ideas from tradition, but when you perform a traditional dance, you present it as it is.

## Evaluating a performance

Ask: Did the dancers keep the rhythm? Were the steps correct and together? Was the costume suitable? Did they show the right feeling and respect?

9.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. use the colour wheel to find complementary and analogous colours;
2. name warm and cool colours and the effects of each;
3. identify emphasis, balance, repetition and unity in an artwork;
4. plan a poster using the elements and principles of design.

## Materials

A colour wheel chart, coloured paper, pencils, printed posters or paintings, paper for planning.

## Starter

Show two pictures of the same scene: one in only warm colours, one in only cool colours. Ask learners how each makes them feel.

## Development

1. Revise the elements: line, shape, form, colour, texture, space. Revise principles: balance, contrast, emphasis, repetition (rhythm), proportion and unity.
2. The colour wheel: primary, secondary and tertiary colours. Warm colours (red, orange, yellow) feel active; cool colours (blue, green, purple) feel calm.
3. Complementary colours are opposites on the wheel (red-green, blue-orange, yellow-purple) and make strong contrast. Analogous colours are neighbours (blue, blue-green, green) and make harmony.
4. Emphasis (focal point): the part of a picture that grabs the eye first, made by size, contrast or position.
5. Repetition makes pattern and rhythm. Unity: all parts belong together. Space and perspective: smaller and higher objects seem further away; overlapping shows depth.
6. Analyse a poster, then plan one.

## Class activity

Groups plan a poster for a school clean-up campaign, deciding the colour scheme, focal point, balance, repetition and lettering.

## Evaluation

1. Name a pair of complementary colours.
2. What is a focal point?
3. What does repeating a shape do in a design?

reading.title: Reading and planning a picture
reading.content:
# Elements and principles of art in use

In JSS 1 you learned the elements of art and some principles of design. Artists use them together. This week we look at colour more closely and at how to plan a picture.

## The colour wheel

The colour wheel arranges the colours in a circle: the **primary** colours (red, yellow, blue), the **secondary** colours (orange, green, purple) and the colours between them.

- **Warm colours:** red, orange, yellow. They feel active, hot and close.
- **Cool colours:** blue, green, purple. They feel calm and distant.

## Colour schemes

- **Complementary colours** are opposite each other on the wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. Placed together they make strong **contrast**, and each makes the other look brighter.
- **Analogous colours** are neighbours on the wheel, such as blue, blue-green and green. They blend smoothly and give a **calm, harmonious** feeling.

## Principles in use

- **Emphasis (focal point):** the part the eye goes to first. An artist makes it larger, brighter, or placed in the centre.
- **Balance:** the weight of the parts is spread so that the picture feels steady. It can be symmetrical (the same on both sides) or asymmetrical.
- **Repetition and rhythm:** repeating a shape, line or colour makes a pattern and leads the eye around the picture.
- **Contrast:** differences, such as dark against light, make parts stand out. Lettering must contrast with its background to be read.
- **Unity:** all the parts belong together because of a shared colour, style or theme.
- **Proportion:** the size of parts compared with one another.

## Showing space

Things look **further away** when they are drawn **smaller**, **higher up the page**, **paler** and **overlapped** by nearer objects.

## Planning a poster

Suppose you are making a poster for a school clean-up campaign.

1. **Colour:** green for nature, with bright yellow for the slogan, which stands out against it.
2. **Emphasis:** a large picture of a child with a broom, placed in the centre.
3. **Balance:** the picture in the middle and the words above and below, in equal weight.
4. **Repetition:** small leaf shapes repeated around the border.
5. **Contrast and unity:** big, clear lettering that contrasts with the background, in the same colours as the picture.

Planning before painting saves time and makes the message clear.

10.lessonNote:
## Objectives

By the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

1. arrange a still life with a good composition;
2. check proportions by measuring with a pencil;
3. draw round objects and their openings using ellipses and guidelines;
4. use tone and mark-making to show smooth and rough textures.

## Materials

Pencils (HB, 2B, 4B, 6B), paper, erasers; a clay pot, a calabash, a mango or orange, a small woven basket; a lamp or window light.

## Starter

Ask learners to look at the still life for a minute and then close their eyes and say how many objects there are and which is tallest. Discuss what they did not notice.

## Development

1. Composition: group objects of different heights, overlap some, make one object the focal point, and fill most of the page.
2. Lighting: use one light source from one side so that the shadows fall the same way.
3. Proportion: hold a pencil at arm's length, with one eye closed, to compare the height and width of each object. Draw lightly and correct.
4. A circle seen from a slight angle looks like an ellipse, as does the opening of a pot. Use a centre line and light guidelines to make both halves match.
5. Tone: use a scale from white through greys to black. Shiny objects have small sharp highlights and strong contrast; rough objects have softer lights and visible texture marks.
6. Mark-making: smooth blending for smooth surfaces; short repeated marks, cross-hatching or dashes for rough ones.

## Class activity

Learners draw a group of three objects from observation, then compare their drawing with a partner's, using the checklist: composition, proportion, tone, texture.

## Evaluation

1. How do you check proportions?
2. What shape is the rim of a pot seen from slightly above?
3. How do you show a rough texture?

## Assignment

reading.title: Drawing what is really there
reading.content:
# Drawing a still life

A **still life** is a drawing or painting of a group of objects arranged on a table. In JSS 1 you drew a single object and shaded it. Now you will draw a group and show how things feel to the touch.

## Composition

The way the objects are arranged on the page is the **composition**.

- Choose objects of **different heights and shapes**: a tall calabash, a round pot, a small mango.
- **Overlap** some of them, so that one is clearly in front of another.
- Make one object the **focal point**, usually the largest or the one in the centre.
- Let the group **fill most of the page** and not leave it empty on one side.

## Lighting

Use **one light source**, such as a window or a lamp, from one side. Every object then has a light side and a shadow side, and the cast shadows all fall the same way.

## Proportion

To check proportion, hold your pencil at arm's length with one eye closed. Measure the height of an object against your pencil, then see how many of those lengths its width is. Draw lightly and correct until the drawing matches.

## Ellipses

A circle seen from the side or slightly above looks like an **ellipse**, a flattened circle. The opening of a pot is an ellipse. To draw it:

1. Draw a light **centre line** down the pot.
2. Draw the ellipse so that both halves are the same.
3. The **bottom** edge of the pot is also curved, more than the top.

## Tone

A **tonal scale** goes from white through greys to black. Use it to show form: light, mid-tones, dark, cast shadow and sometimes **reflected light**, a faint light on the shadow side from a nearby object.

## Showing texture

| Surface | How to draw it |
| --- | --- |
| Smooth and shiny (glazed clay pot) | Blend the pencil smoothly; leave a small, sharp, bright highlight next to a very dark tone |
| Rough and dull (raffia basket) | Short repeated marks, cross-hatching or dashes that follow the weave; softer highlights and less contrast |

## Checking your work

Ask: Is the composition balanced? Are the proportions right? Is there a full range of tones? Can I tell which object is smooth and which is rough?
